newsitem.title: THAILAND: Government to float bonds to help troubled sector.
newsitem.headline: Government to float bonds to help troubled sector.

text.p: Thailand has followed up moves to strengthen its financial sector by unveiling a major fund raising plan to bail out the troubled property projects and telling small, shaky finance houses to merge.

Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on the weekend the government would soon float up to 100 billion baht ($3.87 billion), seven-year, zero-coupon bonds to raise funds to help the property sector weather a four-year slump.

Most finance company executives meeting here welcomed the bail-out scheme, which would inject badly needed liquidity into non-bank financial institutions threatened by non-performing loans to the property sector.

The governor told finance companies that proceeds from the bonds, expected to get cabinet approval this week, would be used for refinancing indebted property projects, giving developers more time to sell them while the market gradually improved.

"This plan, comparing with other measures announced earlier, sounds the most practical in helping the whole industry," said Nives Hemvachiravarakorn, senior executive vice president of Nava Finance and Securities Plc.
Rerngchai said he expected the planned zero-coupon bond issue to be a success as finance institutional buyers could use the bonds as reserves like other government debt instruments.

The governor, backed by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, also told Thailand's 91 finance companies to shape up, saying he expected many of them to merge in the next few years in preparation for greater competition from bigger foreign firms.

"The Bank of Thailand will set guidelines encouraging as many mergers as possible. We will use carrot and stick to induce mergers, giving them incentives including an expanded scope of their licensed business," the governor said.
He said finance firms agreeing to merge may be rewarded with two new bank licenses that the central bank planned to issue later.
"I fully support the merger policy. Finance firms need to be strengthened in order to compete in a globalised environment," said Krairit Uchukanondchai, president of Thana One Plc.

Months of market concern that the property slump would bankrupt troubled finance firms exploded last week when Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank Plc announced a friendly merger, and the government ordered 10 finance houses to raise capital.

The government action triggered public runs on about 15-20 billion baht of finance company deposits, but withdrawals eased on Friday after the central bank said it would guarantee repayment of promissory notes issued by those firms.
The central bank also instructed Thailand's 15 banks and 91 finance companies to set aside 50 billion baht ($1.94 billion) as additional provisions for sub-standard assets within two years.

A foreign analyst estimated that at least 8.8 percent of bank and finance company loans were classified as doubtful or sub-standard assets and that their low quality would deteriorate further as the property sector slump dragged on.
Minister Amnuay said about 10 percent of total bank loans and 25 percent of finance lending went to the property sector, but he stressed that only a portion of these had turned soured.
